chat.about_p1: What we're trying to do: give each jurisdiction a first-pass, directional read on which sectors and which subnational units are the largest sources of methane — a clearer sense of the major emitters — so that a government can prioritise where a real action plan is worth building. This is a triage tool, not a certified inventory.
chat.about_p2: Where the numbers come from: Climate TRACE, an independent nonprofit coalition that models emissions from satellite imagery, remote sensors, and activity data (production volumes, land use, livestock counts) — it is inference from indirect signals, not a network of continuous ground monitors.
chat.about_p3: Key deficiency to keep in mind: satellite instruments pass over a given location periodically, not continuously — so a satellite-derived estimate is closer to a series of snapshots stitched together than to a real-time emissions feed. Estimates also carry wider uncertainty for diffuse sources (small-scale agriculture, informal waste) than for large point sources (oil & gas facilities), and the subnational split itself is a modeled allocation, not a jurisdiction's own self-report.
chat.about_p4: See the full Data & Methods page for the complete picture, including known limitations.
chat.about_title: ℹ️  About this data — what it is, and its limits

chat.s_data_country: In {y}, **{country}** emitted **{total} {unit}** of methane. The top three subnational units ({top3}) together explain **{pct}%** of the national footprint.
chat.s_data_loc: In {y}, **{subject}** emitted **{total} {unit}** of methane (under the *{metric}* framing). That is **{pct}%** of {country}'s national CH₄ total.
chat.s_data_method: Data: Climate TRACE · monthly subnational methane · {range} series. Metric framing: {metric} (multiplier ×{mult}). Uncertainty band ≈ ±15-25% at subunit level.
chat.s_data_pathway: Sequence by abatement density. Highest-density action set in **{sector}**: {actions}.
chat.s_method: Methane (CH₄) is short-lived but extremely potent. Converting CH₄ to CO₂-equivalent depends on the time horizon — that choice changes which sectors look most urgent.
chat.s_method_insight:
For {subject}'s {t} t CH₄ in {y}:

- **GWP100 (×{g100}):** ≈ {v100} t CO₂e — comparable to long-term climate accounting.
- **GWP20 (×{g20}):** ≈ {v20} t CO₂e — reflects near-term warming pressure relevant to 1.5°C pathways.

The GWP20 framing roughly **triples** methane's apparent weight versus GWP100.
chat.s_method_method: IPCC AR6 WG1 Ch.7 Table 7.15 · GWP100 = 27.2 (non-fossil CH₄), GWP20 = 79.7. Values rounded for display. SMAC always discloses which GWP horizon is in use to prevent metric-switching greenwashing.
chat.s_method_pathway: Report both GWP100 and GWP20 side-by-side. Prioritise fast-mitigation, low-cost sources (oil & gas leaks, landfill gas) where GWP20 framing materially changes the cost-benefit.
chat.s_method_policy: Most national inventories report under GWP100 (UNFCCC convention). Subnational decision-making is increasingly using GWP20 to justify near-term methane action — but switching framings without disclosure is itself a greenwashing risk.
chat.s_no_pathway: No pathway data for {country} in this prototype.

chat.s_pathway_first: Highest-priority near-term action: **{action}** in the {sector} sector. Pair with verification (satellite, third-party audit) to preserve credibility.
chat.s_pathway_method: Pathway logic uses IEA Methane Tracker abatement curves + IPCC AR6 WG3 Ch.6 (energy) and Ch.7 (AFOLU). Greenwashing checks: {flags}.
chat.s_pathway_policy: Each pathway must clear a greenwashing audit before it counts toward national pledges.
chat.s_policy: {country}'s methane policy stack combines federal mandates with subnational implementation. Coverage is uneven — strongest in the dominant sector, thinner in agricultural and waste streams.
chat.s_policy_insight: In {y}, **{top3}** together produced **{t} t CH₄** — about **{pct}%** of national methane. Yet only a subset of {unit} have binding instruments beyond the federal floor.
chat.s_policy_method: Policy text retrieved from official registers. Anti-greenwashing flag: {flag}.
chat.s_policy_pathway: Priority gap: align {unit} rules to the dominant emitter. {actions}.
chat.s_trend: Across {range}, **{subject}** shows a **{dir}** trajectory of **{drift}%** in CH₄. The most recent year-on-year change is **{yoy}%**.
chat.s_trend_falling: A falling trajectory does not mean the job is done — sustained reduction requires verification, not self-reporting.
chat.s_trend_insight:
- Peak month: **{peak_m} {peak_y}** — {peak_t} t CH₄
- Low month: **{low_m} {low_y}** — {low_t} t CH₄
- Range ratio (peak/trough): **{ratio}×**
- Annual average drift: **{avg}% / year**
chat.s_trend_method: Trend computed on raw Climate TRACE monthly aggregates. Seasonality not deseasonalised in this view; underlying signal is the inter-annual change.
chat.s_trend_rising: A rising trajectory means current policy is not bending the curve. Subnational instruments may need binding targets, not voluntary measures.

faq.carbon_mapper.a:
**No.** No Carbon Mapper measurements feed any figure on this site — the inventory, rankings and facility tables are all Climate TRACE.

The two answer different questions. Carbon Mapper detects and quantifies individual methane **plumes** from aircraft and satellite overpasses — a snapshot of a specific leak at a specific moment. Climate TRACE estimates **total emissions over time** for every sector, including diffuse sources like agriculture that rarely produce a detectable plume. Plume observations are a powerful way to find and verify super-emitters, but they can't be added up into an annual inventory on their own.

To see plume detections for your jurisdiction, use Carbon Mapper's public portal at [data.carbonmapper.org](https://data.carbonmapper.org/).
faq.chat_ai.a: When an AI model is connected, it writes the answer — but it's given the computed Climate TRACE figures and passages retrieved from SMAC's document library, told to use only those for any number, name or policy, and to say when it's drawing on general knowledge. Sources are listed under each answer. Check anything important against them before using it officially, and please don't enter confidential information.
faq.chat_ai.q: Does the Chat use AI? Can it make things up?
faq.differs.a: Climate TRACE revises historical estimates between releases as its models improve. This site is pinned to the {date} snapshot, so a number here can legitimately differ from what climatetrace.org shows now. That's a version difference, not an error in either place.
faq.differs.q: Why does a figure differ from climatetrace.org today?
faq.enteric.a: Enteric fermentation is methane from livestock digestion — usually the largest agricultural source. Climate TRACE splits cattle into animals **on pasture** (grazing) and animals **in operations** (feedlots and dairies), plus other livestock. The split matters because the levers differ: feed additives and herd management apply very differently to confined versus grazing herds. Use the **Inside a sector** drill-down on the SMAC Members page to see it for your jurisdiction.
faq.enteric.q: What does enteric fermentation "pasture" vs "operation" mean?
faq.global.a: Yes. The **Global View** page covers every state, province and region Climate TRACE estimates — type your jurisdiction's name to see its methane total and trend, sector mix, and its top 20 emitting facilities. It is deliberately simpler than the SMAC Members page, which adds the sub-sector drill-down, existing action plans and policy context. Joining SMAC is free — see **Contact**.
faq.global.q: We're not a SMAC member — can we see our own data?
faq.gwp.a: Both convert methane to CO₂-equivalent. **GWP100 (×{gwp100})** weighs warming over 100 years and is the standard in most national inventories. **GWP20 (×{gwp20})** weighs the first 20 years, when methane's effect is strongest — relevant for near-term targets. The site always labels which one is in use, since switching between them without saying so can make progress look better or worse than it is.
faq.gwp.q: What's the difference between GWP100 and GWP20?
faq.intro: Quick answers to what SMAC members ask most. For the full picture, see Data & Methods; for anything not covered here, see Contact.
faq.inventory.a:
Usually because the two are built differently. An official inventory is typically **bottom-up** — activity data and emission factors compiled by the government, often with local detail Climate TRACE doesn't have. Climate TRACE is **modeled** from remote signals and global asset data, and it allocates national totals down to subnational boundaries. Sector definitions, global warming potentials and reporting years can also differ.

Where a jurisdiction publishes its own inventory, that is usually the more authoritative figure. We've integrated Maryland's state inventory alongside Climate TRACE in the Chat, and we'd like to do the same for others — send yours via **Contact**.
faq.inventory.q: Why doesn't a figure match our official inventory?
faq.languages.a: Yes — use the language menu at the top right: English, 中文, Español, Português, 한국어 and हिन्दी. The whole site switches, and the Chat answers in the language you choose. Two things stay as they are: names of places and facilities, and passages quoted from source documents, which are shown in their original language. Translations are provided for convenience; where wording differs, the English version is authoritative.
faq.languages.q: Can I use the site in my language?
faq.member_observer.a: **Members** ({members}) have formally joined the coalition and committed to its methane goals. **Observers** ({observers}) take part in SMAC convenings and use its resources but haven't made that formal commitment, often because a domestic process is still underway.
faq.member_observer.q: What's the difference between a member and an observer?
faq.official.a: No. It's a **triage tool**: a fast, directional read on which sectors and facilities drive a jurisdiction's methane, to help decide where a mitigation strategy or a deeper verified inventory would have the most impact. It isn't designed for setting binding targets or verifying compliance.
faq.official.q: Is this an official or certified inventory?
faq.partial.a: Because it's a **partial year** — only {n} months are reported so far. Wherever {ny} is shown, the year-over-year change compares the same {n} months of {y}, not the full year, so the comparison isn't distorted. {y} is the latest complete year and the default everywhere.
faq.partial.q: Why does {ny} look so much lower?
faq.plans.a: Plans and strategies a jurisdiction or its agencies have **already published** — SMAC doesn't author them. Where none is on file, the section is labelled **Suggested Starting Actions** instead and lists general best-practice measures for the jurisdiction's largest sectors, which are a starting point, not a plan.
faq.send_data.a: Yes, please. Tell us the jurisdiction, year, sector and what you believe the right figure is — or send your official inventory and we'll work on integrating it. Details are on the **Contact** page.
faq.send_data.q: Can we send our own data or a correction?
faq.source.a: Every emissions figure comes from **Climate TRACE**, an independent nonprofit coalition that models emissions from satellite and remote-sensing signals, facility-level asset data, and statistical models. This site serves the snapshot pulled on **{date}** (API {api}), covering **{range}** at monthly resolution.
faq.source.q: Where do the numbers come from?
faq.title: Frequently asked questions.
faq.top_sources.a: Individual named facilities from Climate TRACE — a specific landfill, plant or mine — ranked by methane. Oil & gas entries are often **field- or basin-level aggregates** rather than a single site. Road transport, forestry and most agriculture aren't listed, because there a "source" is a road segment or grid cell rather than a facility you could contact.
faq.under_construction.a: Some jurisdictions maintain a more detailed official inventory that doesn't yet line up with Climate TRACE. Rather than publish one source as if it were settled, we hold the profile back until the two are reconciled. A newly joined member can also briefly show a "data being added" notice until its figures are merged in.
faq.under_construction.q: Why is a jurisdiction shown as "under construction"?
faq.updates.a: Climate TRACE publishes a new month roughly every month, with about a 60-day lag. This site is refreshed by re-pulling the data periodically rather than live, so the snapshot date above tells you exactly which release you're seeing.
faq.updates.q: How often is the data updated?

methods.coal_note: One grouping decision worth flagging: Climate TRACE already classifies coal-mining under fossil fuels, so that isn't something we moved — it sits in our Fossil Fuel Extraction & Mining category exactly where Climate TRACE puts it. What we did fold in is Climate TRACE's separate mineral-extraction sector (copper, iron, bauxite, quarrying). For methane specifically those contribute essentially nothing — together they account for under 0.02% of the category, and most report zero CH₄ outright — so giving them their own top-level slot would add a visual category that is empty in every jurisdiction. If you are looking at CO₂ rather than methane, that trade-off would not hold.
methods.intro: This tool exists to give SMAC members a fast, first-pass read on where their methane comes from. Concretely, we are trying to do one thing well: get a basic sense of the sources and sectors of methane emissions by jurisdiction, with a clearer sense of the major emitters — enough to point a government toward where a real action plan is worth building. It is not a regulatory-grade monitoring system, a substitute for a certified inventory, or a live sensor feed.
methods.lim1_desc: Every figure is a model output built from satellite and sensor signals plus activity data — not a direct, continuous measurement of methane in the air. Treat it as a well-informed estimate, not a metered reading.
methods.lim2_desc: A satellite passes over any given facility or region only periodically — a handful of overpasses a month, not continuous coverage. Climate TRACE's models stitch these point-in-time observations together with activity data to estimate a monthly total, but the underlying satellite signal is a series of snapshots, not an uninterrupted stream of emissions data. A short-lived spike or lull between overpasses can be missed entirely.
methods.lim2_title: Satellites capture moments, not a continuous feed
methods.lim3_desc: The newest month available is always about two months old, and Climate TRACE regularly revises earlier months (sometimes years back) as methods improve. A number you see today may shift slightly in a future release.
methods.lim4_desc: Large point sources like oil & gas facilities and power plants are estimated with tighter confidence. Diffuse sources — small-scale agriculture, informal waste sites, land-use change — carry wider uncertainty bands, sometimes ±25% or more at the subnational level.
methods.lim4_title: Uncertainty varies a lot by sector
methods.lim5_desc: Attribution of national totals down to states, provinces, or other subnational units is a modeled allocation based on asset locations and administrative boundaries — not a jurisdiction's own self-report or a government-certified inventory.
methods.lim6_desc: Because releases happen monthly with a lag, what you're looking at is closer to a periodic snapshot of the model's best current estimate than to continuous real-time emissions tracking.
methods.lim6_title: A snapshot of modeled totals, not a live feed
methods.lim_title: Read the numbers with these caveats in mind.
methods.method_link_intro: The full sector-by-sector methodology is published openly:
methods.method_link_sub: github.com/climatetracecoalition — the per-sector method docs behind every estimate shown in this tool
methods.snapshot: Which snapshot you're looking at. The figures on this site were pulled from Climate TRACE on {date} (API {api}). Climate TRACE improves its models continuously and revises historical estimates between releases, so a figure here can legitimately differ from climatetrace.org today, or from what this site showed a few months ago. That's a version difference, not an error in either place.
methods.source_p1: Climate TRACE is an independent, nonprofit coalition (satellite operators, universities, and research labs) that estimates greenhouse gas emissions for essentially every country, state/province, and more than 740 million individual facilities and assets worldwide. It does this by combining satellite imagery, remote sensors, and activity data (production volumes, land-use change, livestock counts, and similar) with sector-specific emissions models — it is inference from indirect signals, not a network of continuous ground-truth methane monitors.
methods.source_p2: As of March 2025, Climate TRACE releases a new month of data every month, with roughly a 60-day lag — so the most recent month you can see here is never truly current, and each release also revises prior months as better information comes in.
methods.source_title: Climate TRACE — modeled, not measured directly.
methods.tax_link_sub: climatetrace.org/sectors — definitions, sub-sector lists, and the method docs for how each sector is estimated
methods.tax_p1: Climate TRACE publishes emissions under a detailed taxonomy of {n} activity-level sub-sectors (oil-and-gas-production, enteric-fermentation-cattle-pasture, solid-waste-disposal, and so on), grouped under a set of top-level sectors. This tool rolls those up into {k} broad categories so that a jurisdiction's profile stays readable — but the underlying sub-sector detail is preserved, and it's what drives the Top emitting sources table on the SMAC Members page.
methods.tax_p2: You can browse Climate TRACE's own sector definitions — including the methodology documentation behind each one — on their site:
methods.tax_title: How Climate TRACE's sectors map to ours.
methods.three_1: Satellite and remote-sensing signals — direct observation of plumes, thermal signatures, land cover and activity indicators.
methods.three_2: Global asset-level data — the locations of individual facilities, their size, their technology and operating characteristics. This is what makes a facility-by-facility ranking possible at all, rather than a national total split by population or GDP.
methods.three_3: Machine learning and other statistical models — used to fill gaps where direct observation isn't available, and to convert observed activity into an emissions estimate.
methods.three_intro: Three things go into those estimates, and it's worth being precise about the mix rather than calling it all “satellite data”:
methods.title: What this tool is — and isn't.
methods.use_p1: Use this tool to get a directional answer to three questions for your jurisdiction: which sectors dominate our methane profile, which subnational units and facilities are the largest contributors, and where the biggest opportunities for decarbonization are. That's enough to tell you where a mitigation strategy or a deeper, verified inventory effort would have the most impact.
methods.use_p2: There's a second use worth knowing about. Official inventories are published in multi-year cycles, so there is usually a long gap between the last verified figure and the present. Because Climate TRACE updates continuously, it can show how emissions have moved between inventories, or while an inventory update is still underway — which means it can give an early read on whether a methane abatement action is working before the next official inventory would confirm it.
methods.use_p3: It is deliberately not designed to set binding targets, verify compliance, or replace a jurisdiction's own regulatory inventory — for that, pair this with facility-level verification and your own reporting processes.
methods.use_title: Good for triage. Not a substitute for an audit.
methods.wrong: Think a number here is wrong? Tell us. Where a jurisdiction publishes its own inventory, that is usually the more authoritative figure, and we would rather integrate it than have this tool quietly disagree with it. See the Contact page for how to send a correction or an inventory.
overview.about_body: Worldwide, states and provinces have the authority and expertise to slash methane emissions and combat climate change. Members of the Subnational Methane Action Coalition (SMAC) are leading the way.
overview.about_title: Leading the world toward fast methane action.
overview.does_body: Each jurisdiction has different needs. Whether a government is new to methane efforts or already a world leader, SMAC helps officials craft strong methane policies and gain global recognition for their efforts.
overview.fn1_desc: Through an extensive network of methane experts, SMAC helps governments build customized methane strategies to meet their needs.
overview.fn2_desc: Through SMAC, governments identify key sources of methane, including through low-cost technologies and publicly available satellite data.
overview.fn3_desc: Working alongside industry, SMAC tracks and facilitates innovative methane initiatives at oil and gas operations, farms, landfills, and other facilities.
overview.fn4_desc: SMAC builds international collaborations to exchange model policies, laws, and rules.
overview.fn5_desc: Through SMAC, governments are positioned to maximize the social, economic, and health benefits of methane action.
overview.guide_chat_desc: Ask in plain language — in any of the site's languages. Answers are grounded in the Climate TRACE figures for the jurisdiction you select and in SMAC's library of plans and policy documents, with the sources shown.
overview.guide_chat_q: What policy options fit our largest sources?
overview.guide_compare_desc: Put two jurisdictions — or the same one in two years — side by side: sector breakdown, data table, and how the sector mix has shifted since 2021.
overview.guide_compare_q: How does our profile differ from a peer's?
overview.guide_contact_desc: Join SMAC, reach the research team, or send a correction or your own inventory so we can integrate it.
overview.guide_contact_q: A number looks wrong — who do we tell?
overview.guide_faq_desc: Short answers to the questions members ask most — e.g. whether Carbon Mapper data is included, why a figure differs from an official inventory.

overview.guide_methods_desc: Where the numbers come from, how Climate TRACE's sectors map to ours, and the known limitations — read this before quoting a figure.
overview.guide_methods_q: How much should we trust this number?
overview.guide_smac_desc: Pick any SMAC member or observer to see its methane total and trend, sector mix, a sub-sector drill-down (e.g. enteric fermentation), the top 20 emitting facilities on a map, and the action plans it has already published.
overview.guide_smac_q: How much methane do we emit, and from where?
overview.hero_body: The SMAC Methane Inventory Tool tracks methane emissions across every actual Subnational Methane Action Coalition member and observer jurisdiction — {n} states, provinces, and regions across {c} countries — from 2021 through 2026, paired with a chat that reasons through IPCC GWP frameworks and policy context.
overview.imperative_p1: Methane is a colorless, combustible gas that has caused nearly one-third of Earth's warming. In the short term, one ton of methane traps 80 times more heat than one ton of carbon dioxide. Since captured methane can be used for fuel, methane solutions are often profitable.
overview.imperative_p2: States and provinces are uniquely positioned to lead the fight against methane emissions. SMAC provides a platform that helps governments gain access to technical and policy resources while learning from each other. Joining SMAC is always free.
overview.members_body: Members are jurisdictions that have formally joined the coalition and committed to its methane goals. Observers participate in SMAC convenings and have access to its technical and policy resources, but have not made that formal commitment — often because a domestic process is still underway. Both appear throughout this tool; observer status is labelled wherever a jurisdiction is shown.
overview.new_here: New here? Start with Data & Methods — what this data is, and where it falls short.
overview.step1_desc: Monthly methane data from Climate TRACE across SMAC countries, down to subnational units.
overview.step2_desc: Validate time trends, detect unusual changes, and flag uncertainty at the local level.
overview.step3_desc: Convert CH₄ into CO₂e using IPCC GWP100 and GWP20, and identify emission hotspots.
overview.step4_desc: AI chat connects data with policy context and explains what is happening and why.
overview.step5_desc: Suggest mitigation pathways based on impact, while flagging potential greenwashing risks.

policy.ARG.0.desc: Sectoral targets for agriculture, energy, waste.
policy.ARG.0.name: National Climate Plan 2030
policy.ARG.1.desc: Major shale gas play — methane intensity is a watch item.
policy.ARG.1.name: Vaca Muerta development
policy.ARG.2.name: Provincial agricultural extension
policy.ARG.summary: Argentina's methane is dominated by enteric fermentation in Buenos Aires Province, Santa Fe, and Córdoba, with growing oil & gas methane from Neuquén.
policy.BOL.summary: Profile content for Bolivia is being prepared as SMAC onboarding continues — Santa Cruz joined as a member. Emissions data and curated policy detail will populate here once available.
policy.BRA.0.desc: Federal low-carbon agriculture plan; integrated crop-livestock-forest systems.
policy.BRA.0.name: Plano ABC+ (2020–2030)
policy.BRA.1.desc: Brazil committed to a 30% methane reduction by 2030 from 2020 levels.
policy.BRA.1.name: Global Methane Pledge
policy.BRA.2.desc: Sectoral plans implemented by states; Pará, Mato Grosso, and São Paulo carry most of the methane abatement obligation.
policy.BRA.2.name: PNMC (National Climate Policy)
policy.BRA.summary: Brazil's methane profile is overwhelmingly agricultural — enteric fermentation from the world's second-largest cattle herd, plus land-use-related emissions concentrated in the Amazon and Cerrado states.
policy.CAN.0.desc: Targeting a 75% reduction in oil & gas methane by 2030 from 2012 levels — the most ambitious national target.
policy.CAN.0.name: Federal Methane Regs (2023 amendments)
policy.CAN.1.desc: Alberta, BC, and Saskatchewan run provincial regimes deemed equivalent to the federal rules.
policy.CAN.1.name: Equivalency Agreements
policy.CAN.2.desc: Proposed rules to mandate landfill gas capture at large municipal sites.
policy.CAN.2.name: Federal Landfill Methane Regs
policy.CAN.summary: Canada is a small absolute emitter but methane-intensive on a per-barrel basis. Alberta and British Columbia carry most of the upstream load; agricultural methane is concentrated in the Prairie provinces.
policy.CHN.summary: Profile content for China is being prepared as SMAC onboarding continues — Beijing joined as an observer. Emissions data and curated policy detail will populate here once available.
policy.DEU.0.desc: Binding LDAR, venting and flaring limits, import standards from 2027.
policy.DEU.0.name: EU Methane Regulation (2024)
policy.DEU.1.desc: Sectoral targets including waste and agriculture.
policy.DEU.1.name: Federal Climate Protection Act
policy.DEU.2.desc: Bavaria, Lower Saxony lead on agricultural methane via biogas capture.
policy.DEU.2.name: Bundesländer programs
policy.DEU.summary: Germany's methane is driven by agriculture and waste; oil & gas is small. EU-wide regulation now sets the pace.
policy.ESP.0.name: Climate Change and Energy Transition Law (2021)
policy.ESP.1.desc: Now applies; LDAR and import standards.
policy.ESP.1.name: EU Methane Regulation
policy.ESP.2.desc: Galicia, Castile and León lead on agricultural methane.
policy.ESP.2.name: Autonomous-community plans
policy.ESP.summary: Spain's methane is split across agriculture, waste, and a small oil & gas share. Catalonia and Andalusia dominate waste-sector methane.
policy.IDN.summary: Profile content for Indonesia is being prepared as SMAC onboarding continues — Palembang and West Java joined as members. Emissions data and curated policy detail will populate here once available.
policy.IND.0.desc: Biogas capture from cattle manure; rolling out across rural India.
policy.IND.0.name: GOBARdhan Scheme
policy.IND.1.desc: Eight missions covering agriculture, water, sustainable habitat.
policy.IND.1.name: National Action Plan on Climate Change
policy.IND.2.desc: Punjab, Haryana drive rice-paddy methane decisions; Uttar Pradesh leads on cattle.
policy.IND.2.name: State agricultural plans
policy.IND.summary: Methane in India is dominated by enteric fermentation and rice cultivation. Subnational variation tracks agro-ecological zones.
policy.ITA.summary: Profile content for Italy is being prepared as SMAC onboarding continues — Lombardy and Emilia-Romagna joined as observers. Emissions data and curated policy detail will populate here once available.
policy.KOR.0.name: Framework Act on Carbon Neutrality (2022)
policy.KOR.1.desc: National emissions trading covers some methane sources.
policy.KOR.1.name: K-ETS
policy.KOR.2.desc: Mandatory landfill gas capture at major sites.
policy.KOR.2.name: Waste sector targets
policy.KOR.summary: Korea's methane is dominated by waste and a smaller agricultural share. Centralised regulation, limited subnational variation.
policy.MEX.0.desc: Methane control in upstream oil & gas (suspended in 2024 — major regulatory gap).
policy.MEX.0.name: NOM-EM-001-ASEA-2017
policy.MEX.1.desc: Sets sectoral targets but enforcement is uneven.
policy.MEX.1.name: General Climate Change Law
policy.MEX.2.desc: Mexico signed but has not finalised an implementation plan.
policy.MEX.2.name: Global Methane Pledge
policy.MEX.summary: Mexico has substantial oil & gas methane (Veracruz, Tabasco, Campeche) plus agricultural methane in the central highlands. Regulatory enforcement is the binding constraint, not data.
policy.NGA.0.desc: Plan to monetise associated gas and reduce flaring.
policy.NGA.0.name: Decade of Gas (2021–2030)
policy.NGA.1.desc: Auctions of flare-gas access to third-party developers.
policy.NGA.1.name: Flare Gas Commercialisation Programme
policy.NGA.2.desc: Establishes National Council on Climate Change.
policy.NGA.2.name: Climate Change Act 2021
policy.NGA.summary: Nigeria's methane is split between Niger Delta oil & gas flaring/venting and agricultural methane in the northern states. Flaring is the headline issue.
policy.USA.0.desc: Federal performance standards for new and existing oil & gas sources; LDAR, flaring restrictions, pneumatic device retrofits.
policy.USA.0.name: EPA OOOOb/c (2024)
policy.USA.1.desc: Charge of up to $1,500/tonne on facilities exceeding intensity thresholds; first methane fee in any country.
policy.USA.1.name: IRA §136 — Methane Emissions Reduction Program
policy.USA.2.desc: Colorado intensity standard, New Mexico waste rule, California cap-and-invest, Pennsylvania VOC rule. Strong subnational variation.
policy.USA.2.name: State rules
policy.USA.summary: The world's largest oil & gas producer carries a methane footprint dominated by upstream and midstream operations, with Texas, Pennsylvania, and Louisiana driving most of the variance. Federal rules set a floor; state rules drive the ceiling.
policy.ZAF.0.desc: Statutory carbon budgets, sector emission targets.
policy.ZAF.0.name: Climate Change Act (2024)
policy.ZAF.1.desc: Now applies to methane on a CO₂e basis.
policy.ZAF.1.name: Carbon Tax
policy.ZAF.2.name: Just Energy Transition Partnership
policy.ZAF.summary: South Africa's methane is dominated by coal mining (Mpumalanga) and waste. Coal mine methane is a focal mitigation opportunity.

profile.ct_map: View {loc} source map on Climate TRACE
profile.docs_note: excerpts retrieved from {loc}'s own documents in our library
profile.drill_note: Climate TRACE sub-sectors. "Pasture" vs "operation" separates grazing cattle from cattle in feedlots and dairies — the two call for different mitigation levers.
profile.fac_note: individual emitting assets from Climate TRACE, ranked by methane. Waste, power, manufacturing and mineral-extraction rows are genuine single sites (a named landfill, a named plant). Oil & gas rows are often field- or basin-level aggregates rather than one wellpad — e.g. an entry covering a whole production play — so treat those as "where to look" rather than "which gate to knock on". Road transport, forestry and most agriculture are excluded entirely, because there an emissions source is a road segment or grid cell, not a site.
profile.help_gwp100: {y} methane converted to CO₂-equivalent using the 100-year Global Warming Potential (×{f}) — the standard used in most national inventories and long-term climate accounting.
profile.help_gwp20: {y} methane converted to CO₂-equivalent using the 20-year Global Warming Potential (×{f}) — reflects methane's much stronger near-term warming effect, relevant for near-term (e.g. 2030/2050) climate targets.
profile.help_partial: {loc} emitted this over the first {n} months of {y} — the only months reported so far. The change below compares those same {n} months in {py}, not the full prior year, because comparing a part-year against a full year would show a large false drop.
profile.help_rank: {loc}'s position when every one of the {n} SMAC member/observer jurisdictions worldwide is ranked by {y} methane emissions, #1 = highest. The percentage is {loc}'s share of the combined total that all {n} SMAC jurisdictions emitted together in {y} — e.g. "7.3%" means this one jurisdiction accounts for 7.3% of everything the whole SMAC coalition emitted that year.
profile.help_total: Total methane {loc} emitted in {y}, in million tonnes (Mt). The small number below is the year-over-year change vs {py}.
profile.kept_snapshot: Emissions figures for {loc} are from the {old} Climate TRACE snapshot: they use its urban-area boundary, which the current API can't be queried by. Facility data is current ({new}).
profile.no_plan_data: No {y} data yet for {loc} to build an action plan from.

profile.uc_body: We've held this profile back rather than publish the Climate TRACE estimate on its own, because {loc} maintains a more granular official inventory and the two do not yet line up. Publishing one without reconciling the other would imply a settled figure that does not exist yet.
